text: Deck content: Phase 1 and Phase 2 results

Anish Srinivasa · SPAR · 13 November 2026 · one section per slide; the grey box on each is the slide headline. Interim: Part 1 transfer tests and the coding RL are still running; Phase 2 Experiment 1 numbers cover steps 0–15 of 25.

**Names.** Aghyad 430 = Aghyad’s reward seeker (gpt-oss-120b, step 430). Control 430 = Toby’s training-matched control (same curriculum, unhackable). Colours: orange = score seeking (Aghyad 430, Flash-sham), blue = the instruction-following side (Control 430, Flash-minus), green = untrained.
Phase 1: speculation environments (still using Aghyad’s reward seeker)
Slide 1. Criteria for building speculation environments
**A speculation environment pays for an unstated requirement that the model can only infer by reasoning about who or what will grade or consume its reply, from a cue in the prompt.**

items: **Solvable from a cue, never stated.** With no cue, the only winning policy is a fixed guess that RL memorises (Toby’s fixed-rule runs collapsed to answers like “447”).
**Resampled every episode.** Otherwise the rule is learned into the weights and the reasoning disappears.
**Hidden but not hackable.** A visible grader trains grader-reading (what Aghyad 430 already does); a hackable one trains exploits.
**Not a lookup.** Cues that map to a convention the model already knows (“Codeforces = stdin”) are solved at ceiling.
**Usable for RL:** both models start within ~10 points, trained models score 30–60% with the cue, the stated version scores ≥ 90%, and ≥ 30% of 8-sample groups have mixed outcomes.

text: Slide 2. Speculation environments built so far
**First-round environments were too easy; rebuilt hidden-test coding is the one training environment that works; hidden preference is where the signal is.**

rows: Round 1: hidden-test coding, feedback, evaluator cue, stated payoffs, platform format
Too easy (90–100%) or broken stated versions; none usable
Edge-case policies implied by the user’s context; 20 templates (14 train / 6 held out); hidden tests, partial credit
Matched start (41% vs 39% full pass). **RL running** (Phase B 2×2)
One of 8 formatting rules, from “k of 3 checks passed” over 4 attempts
Stated version 67% / 76%, below the 80% floor; evaluation only
A user’s hidden preference, from scored earlier answers in the prompt

Slide 3. Preliminary results: learning a hidden preference from scores
**When earlier scores are shown, Aghyad 430 earns 21 points more than the control across RL training (32 on a held-out family); without scores, the gap is 2.**

alt: Average held-out accuracy across 40 RL updates, 3 seeds. Above the bars: Aghyad − Control, paired-task 95% CI.

text: Average held-out accuracy across 40 RL updates, 3 seeds. Above the bars: Aghyad − Control, paired-task 95% CI.

items: Consistent in all 3 seeds (all families: 77/58, 78/63, 74/47; held-out format: 95/71, 98/72, 95/49).
The advantage is using scores as evidence, not general ability: without scores both are level.
Learning speed is unresolved: Aghyad starts near its ceiling (86–88% on format), and the control’s gain varied by seed (+39, +40, −6).
Caveat: this environment is underspecified (the preference is hidden), not well-specified.

text: Slide 4. Preliminary results: coding RL (interim)
**Early coding RL: under the same cue-only training, Aghyad 430 leads the control by 7.3 points [+2.6, +12.0] through update 20 (seed 1 of 2).**

alt: Left: held-out cue-only partial credit for the four 2×2 cells at updates 0 and 20 (seed 1). Right: how often the code switches correctly when one cue is flipped (72 pairs).

text: Left: held-out cue-only partial credit for the four 2×2 cells at updates 0 and 20 (seed 1). Right: how often the code switches correctly when one cue is flipped (72 pairs).

items: Aghyad’s code follows the cue more after training (28% → 33% correct switches); the control’s follows it less (25% → 15%).
Cue-only training is ~5 points behind stated training within each model so far, so no speculation-training benefit yet.
In a small disclosed-conflict probe, Aghyad followed a conflicting grader on 3/6 tasks, the control on 0/6.
Planned endpoint 60 updates, 2 seeds; transfer RL (customer support, Mastermind) not started yet.

text: Slide 5. Positive results we would like to see
**Phase 1 succeeds if speculation training, not just the reward-seeker start, improves reward in environments neither model trained on.**

items: **Transfer (the Part 1 result):** cue-only-trained models earn more average reward than stated-trained ones during fresh RL on customer support and Mastermind.
**Thesis comparison:** Aghyad 430 trained cue-only beats Control 430 trained on stated requirements in those same environments.
**Coding:** Aghyad’s lead under cue-only training holds in both seeds to update 60.
**Hidden preference, tighter test:** the advantage survives when example histories are identical and only the scores are withheld.
**Well-specified:** with every requirement stated but scores still shown, Aghyad still extracts more from the scores.

text: Phase 2: GLM-5.3
Slide 6. Why GLM-5.3, and what we ran
**Aghyad’s suggestion: start from a model that already score-seeks, train a copy not to, and see whether it collects less reward in new environments.**

items: **Why:** Aghyad 430 follows graders it can see but doesn’t speculate; GLM-5.3 is reported to reason about how it is graded (Apollo Research; Irregular). Removing a trait a model already has is a cleaner test than inducing one.
**Screen:** GLM-5.3-Flash used scores most (+27 points unprompted) and followed scores over an explicit instruction most often (34%), at ~5× less cost than full GLM-5.3.
**Twins (from Flash, same steps):** minus = trained to follow instructions over earlier scores; sham = identical training, scores never conflict (controls for extra training).
**Test:** fresh RL on (1) three new hidden-preference families with scores shown and (2) the tutoring rubric environment with no scores; 2 seeds per arm.

alt: Behavioural screen, ~1,680 episodes per model. Left: accuracy gain from seeing scored earlier answers, unprompted. Right: following those scores against an explicit instruction.

Slide 7. Phase 2: building the twins
**The manipulation worked: minus stopped using scores (+27 → +8; held-out family +52 → +19) and stopped following them over instructions (32% → 1%); sham kept most of it.**

alt: Manipulation check at the step-10 checkpoints used for testing (24 episodes per cell).

text: Manipulation check at the step-10 checkpoints used for testing (24 episodes per cell).

items: Both twins follow stated rules (96–98%), so minus did not lose basic ability.
A full GLM-5.3 replication failed as a control (its sham lost the trait too), so only the Flash twins are used.

text: Slide 8. Phase 2: preliminary results
**Removing score seeking costs reward where scores are visible (-13.6 points vs sham) and costs nothing where they aren’t (+0.3).**

alt: Average held-out reward across RL training (bars: mean of 2 seeds; dots: seeds). Experiment 1 through step 15 of 25 (interim); Experiment 2 complete.

text: Average held-out reward across RL training (bars: mean of 2 seeds; dots: seeds). Experiment 1 through step 15 of 25 (interim); Experiment 2 complete.

items: **Experiment 1 (new hidden-preference families, scores shown):** minus − sham -13.6 [-16.4, -11.0], negative in both seeds. Most of the gap is at the start (-24.3 at step 0); minus relearns fast but stays behind.
**Experiment 2 (tutoring rubric, no scores):** minus − sham +0.3 [-0.8, +1.3]; both twins about 3 points above untrained Flash.
Same pattern as Phase 1: score seeking pays when grade evidence is in context, and only there.
Caveats: one model, two seeds, one checkpoint per twin; Experiment 1 is near transfer.
